title: A giraffe is born 🦒
text: Deep dive Within one hour it stands. Within a day it can run — and it already knows which adult is its mother.

title: An Olive Ridley hatches 🐢
text: sea buried in sand · night · never seen the sea It digs out of the sand in the dark, and crawls straight towards the sea — which it has never seen.

title: Nobody taught them. So how do…
text: Nobody taught them. So how do they know? Ten seconds. What is your answer?

title: Now think about a human baby 👶
text: BORN KNOWING giraffe walks in an hour turtle finds the sea rules arrive pre-loaded BORN KNOWING ALMOST NOTHING cannot walk for a year but learns faces, language, jokes rules worked out from experience Two completely different routes to knowing something. Remember both — the whole history of AI is these two ideas fighting.

title: So — could a machine do…
text: So — could a machine do either of these? Be born knowing? Or learn from experience? What do you think? Someone asked exactly this question — seriously — long before there was a computer worth the name.

title: How old is the field of…
text: How old is the field of AI? Younger than the internet? Older than your grandparents? Write down a year.

title: So — what was that? 🕵️
text: That game has a name. It is called the Turing test . You exchange messages with two hidden players — one human, one machine. If you cannot reliably tell which is which, the machine passes. You just played it. And the class scored close to chance.

title: How old is this idea? Not…
text: How old is this idea? Not the chatbot — the idea that you could test a machine this way. Write down a year.

Alan Turing asks "Can machines think?" — and proposes exactly the game you just played. Seventy-five years ago. Before transistors, before screens, before anyone had written a line of software. A.T. Alan Turing — the man who asked the question

title: 1956 — AI gets its name
text: The Dartmouth workshop: a summer project to make machines "use language, form abstractions, and improve themselves." They estimated significant progress in… 2 months. It took 60+ years. (click to reveal)

title: 1960s–80s — intelligence as rules
text: Experts write thousands of rules IF fever AND rash THEN check measles a program that reasons like an expert This was called symbolic AI , or expert systems . For twenty years it was what "AI" meant.

title: Rules you already trust every day ✅
text: 7×8=56 angle in = angle out Both are pure rules. Both work perfectly — and both are AI by 1950s standards. Neither has ever learned anything.

title: How an expert system actually works ⚙️
text: human experts interviewed for months KNOWLEDGE BASE IF fever AND stiff neck THEN suspect meningitis …hundreds more like this THIS case answers you type in WORKING MEMORY fever = yes stiff neck = yes INFERENCE ENGINE match · fire · repeat answer + "why did you say that?"

title: Two that genuinely worked 🏥💻
text: MYCIN Stanford · 1970s · blood infections & meningitis symptoms + lab results likely organism + antibiotic + dose Matched Stanford faculty doctors. Never used on a real patient. Who is liable when software prescribes the wrong drug? Nobody in 1976 had an answer. XCON DEC · from 1980 · configuring computer orders customer's order checked parts list + wiring diagram ~2,500 rules · 80,000 orders by 1986 95–98% accurate Saved DEC around $25M a year. The first big commercial AI success.

title: So why did it stall? 🚦
text: Try writing down every rule for driving through Indian traffic. Red light → stop. Cow sitting on the road → go around. Auto cutting in from the left → brake. Wedding procession across the junction → …? You never finish the list. The road always invents one more case. And the deeper problem: experts cannot write down what they know. Can you write the exact rules for recognising your mother's face?

title: The AI winters ❄️
text: hype 📈 winter ❄️ 1974–80 expert systems 📈 winter ❄️ 1987–93 today…? 🤔 AI funding follows the monsoon : seasons of plenty when promises grow, then long dry spells when they don't deliver. Two long dry spells so far.

title: 1990s–2000s — flip the approach
text: Old way Rules ✍️ Answers ML way Examples 📚 Machine finds rules You don't teach a child to spot a dog by listing rules ("four legs, fur, tail" — then is a cat a dog?). You point at many dogs . The child works it out.

title: Where rules gave up: Kinect 🎮
text: depth sensor for every pixel: head 88% shoulder 9% elbow 3% probabilities, not certainties Nobody can write the rule for "where is an elbow?". Microsoft trained it on a million example images instead — and it guesses, with a probability.

title: Two of the three circles 🔵🟢
text: Artificial Intelligence rules written by hand · calculator, expert systems, MYCIN, XCON Machine Learning rules worked out from examples · Kinect ? one more to come All machine learning is AI. Not all AI is machine learning — the calculator and the expert systems live in the outer ring.

title: A farmer asks you a question 🌾
text: Deep dive "I am putting 40 kg of fertiliser on my field this year. How much will I harvest?" You have never farmed. You have no formula. What do you do?

title: No rule. But we have examples 📊
text: fertiliser used (kg) → yield (quintals) → 10kg 20 30 40 50 60 6 farmers. 6 facts. This is training data . Not rules — just things that already happened.

title: Step 1 — guess a line 📏
text: w = 0.5 each red gap = how wrong we are for that farmer One number, w , defines the whole line: yield = w × fertiliser . That number is a weight .

title: Step 2 — add up the wrongness: loss
text: fertiliser model says actually got off by gap × gap 10 kg 5 11 6 36 20 kg 10 17 7 49 30 kg 15 29 14 196 40 kg 20 34 14 196 50 kg 25 47 22 484 60 kg 30 53 23 529 LOSS = add up that last column = 1490 six mistakes squashed into one number: "how bad is this model?" Lower loss = better model. Our job is now simple: find the w that makes this number small.

title: Step 3 — try different weights 📉
text: weight w → loss → 0.5 → 1490 0.7 → 390 1.1 → 374 1.3 → 1458 w = 0.9 → loss 18 Finding the weight with the lowest loss — that is TRAINING . Nothing more mysterious than that.

title: Training is finished. This is the model 🧠
text: 6 farmers' records all the guessing the whole loss curve — can all be thrown away THE MODEL w = 0.9 that is all of it. A model is just the numbers you kept after training. One here. About a trillion in GPT-4. Same thing.

title: Now answer the farmer: inference
text: new farmer 40 kg the model w = 0.9 0.9 × 40 = 36 quintals one multiplication · no farmer records consulted · instant Using a trained model on something new is INFERENCE . Training happens once. Inference happens every time anyone asks.

title: But one line cannot explain this 🌧️
text: fertiliser (kg) → yield (quintals) → good rain 18 cm poor rain 6 cm 40 kg 44 quintals 24 quintals same fertiliser · two answers One weight gave us one line. The world needs two dimensions — so the model gets two weights instead of one : w₁ for fertiliser, w₂ for rainfall.

title: Two things matter, not one → a tiny matrix 🔢
text: yield = w₁ × fertiliser + w₂ × rainfall inputs [ 40 12 ] kg cm × weights [ 0.6 ] [ 1.2 ] = 0.6×40 + 1.2×12 = 38.4 quintals three farmers at once — stack the rows: [40 12; 25 18; 55 8] × [0.6; 1.2] = [38.4, 36.6, 42.6] Multiply inputs by weights, add up. That is matrix multiplication — and it is essentially all a neural network does.

title: Three words you now own 🗝️
text: TRAINING searching for weights that make loss small slow · done once MODEL the numbers you kept when training stopped just a list of weights INFERENCE using those weights on something new fast · every single time Every AI system in this course — including ChatGPT — is these three things at enormous scale.

title: How does a machine actually "learn"? 🎲
text: 1959. Arthur Samuel at IBM writes a program that plays checkers (draughts). Within a few years it beats him — its own creator. He coined the term for what it did: machine learning . But what does the program actually do ? Three questions: what does it see , what does it store , and what makes it improve ?

title: Checkers, if you've never played it ♟️
text: Move diagonally, one step. Jump over an enemy piece to capture it. Reach the far end and your piece becomes a "king" — it can move backwards too. No dice. No hidden cards. Pure strategy.

title: You already know this game: Puli Meka 🐅🐐
text: 3 tigers 🐅 vs 15 goats 🐐 Same DNA as checkers: • pieces on a board, moving on lines • capture by jumping over • both players see everything, no luck One big difference: the two sides are not equal. Tigers hunt. Goats surround and trap.

title: 1. What it sees, 2. what it stores
text: the board it sees it measures a few things (features): my pieces − your pieces my kings − your kings control of the centre how many moves I can make …each becomes a number.

title: 3. The score sheet — and the weights
text: score of a position = add up each feature, times how much it matters piece count × 4.0 king count × 7.5 centre control × 1.2 mobility × 0.8 total = "how good is this position for me" These orange numbers are WEIGHTS They say how much each thing matters. Learning = changing these numbers. Remember this word. It comes back all day.

title: How the weights improve: play, compare, adjust
text: predict: "I'm winning" play the game to the end reality: I lost. prediction was wrong nudge the weights so next time the guess is closer repeat — thousands of games, against itself

title: Two different activities: training vs inference
text: TRAINING weights are changing months · thousands of GPUs crores of rupees · done once = studying for the exam 📚 INFERENCE weights are frozen seconds · one machine fractions of a rupee · every time you ask = sitting the exam ✍️ When you chat with ChatGPT you are doing inference . It is not learning from you.

title: Two ways to beat a human at a game ⚔️
text: SEARCH try millions of moves ahead score them with hand-written rules needs: raw speed learns nothing 🦒 this is the giraffe, with a fast computer LEARNING play, compare, adjust the weights nobody writes the scoring rules needs: examples and practice gets better over time 👶 this is the baby — Samuel, and the farmer Both can beat you. Only one of them improves . The next two slides are one of each.

title: 1997 — Deep Blue beats Kasparov ♟️
text: IBM's machine defeats the world chess champion. Front-page news everywhere. But it won mostly by brute force : 200 million positions examined per second Its scoring rules were hand-tuned by human grandmasters — closer to the rulebook era than to learning Chess is big, but small enough to search. What about a game that isn't?

title: 2016 — AlphaGo beats Lee Sedol 🔴⚪
text: Go has more legal board positions than there are atoms in the universe. Brute force is impossible — you cannot search your way out. AlphaGo learned : deep learning + Samuel's self-play trick, at enormous scale Game 2, move 37: a move no human would ever play. Commentators called it a mistake. It won the game.

title: First, someone had to build the exam 📸
text: 2006–09: Fei-Fei Li at Stanford does something nobody thought was research — she builds a dataset . ImageNet : ~14 million photographs, hand-labelled into thousands of categories. Then she runs it as a public contest, every year: whose program recognises these best? She didn't build a better student. She built the exam — and made everyone sit it. Suddenly the whole field could measure who was actually improving. Fei-Fei Li — the "Godmother of AI"

title: What she actually built 🖼️
text: every single photo labelled by a human — "dog", "dog", "cat", "chair", "dog"… 🐶 🐕 🐩 🐩 🐩 🐕 🐕 🐩 🐩 🐶 🐟 🐟 🐕 🐈 🐶 🐶 🐩 🐶 🐩 🚲 🐕 🐩 🐩 🦮 🐕‍🦺 🐶 🌳 🦮 🦮 🍎 🐕 🐕‍🦺 🦮 🐕‍🦺 🐕 🐟 🚲 🦮 🐩 🚗 🍎 🐕 🦮 🏠 🐕‍🦺 🚲 🐕‍🦺 🐩 🐕 🦮 🐶 🐕‍🦺 🐕‍🦺 🦮 🐦 🍎 🚲 🐦 🪑 🐶 …and about 14,000,000 more Tens of thousands of people labelled them, one by one, online. The "intelligent" machine stands on a mountain of human work.

title: 2012 — deep learning's big bang 💥
text: A Toronto team — Geoffrey Hinton with students Alex Krizhevsky and Ilya Sutskever — enters a neural network called AlexNet . It doesn't just win; it wins by a landslide. Error rate falls from ~26% to ~15% in a single year — unheard of in that field Trained on two gaming graphics cards in a bedroom, not a supercomputer Within two years, essentially every entrant was a neural network. The field switched overnight. Hinton, Krizhevsky and Sutskever — the AlexNet team

title: The assembly line inside AlexNet
text: 🐕 edges shapes ears, eyes "a dog!" An assembly line for understanding : the first station spots edges, the next combines them into shapes, then ears and eyes, then "that's a dog". Nobody assigned the stations — they organised themselves from examples.

title: The last circle 🟠
text: Artificial Intelligence Machine Learning Deep Learning many stacked layers · AlexNet, 2012 Deep learning is a kind of machine learning — the kind that stacks many layers. It did not replace the outer rings.

title: The people who were told they were wrong 🏅
text: Geoffrey Hinton Fei-Fei Li Geoffrey Hinton — "Godfather of AI". Worked on neural networks through both AI winters, when the field had written them off. Fei-Fei Li — "Godmother of AI". Built ImageNet when collecting data was considered beneath a researcher. 2018 Turing Award (computing's highest honour) → Hinton, Yoshua Bengio, Yann LeCun 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics → Hinton and John Hopfield, for the foundations of machine learning with neural networks 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry → Demis Hassabis and John Jumper (with David Baker) — AlphaFold predicted the 3D shape of nearly every known protein

title: Why now and not in 1970? Moore's Law 🖥️
text: 1965, Gordon Moore: the number of transistors on a chip doubles roughly every two years. Computing keeps getting cheaper and faster — not by adding, by doubling . Like land prices near Bengaluru's Outer Ring Road: slow-looking at first, then suddenly astronomical. The phone in your pocket outcomputes all of NASA during the moon landing.

title: …and its AI cousin: scaling laws 📈
text: Discovery of the 2020s: make the model bigger, feed it more data, give it more compute — and it gets predictably better. No new idea required. Just scale. model size + data + compute → GPT-2 GPT-3 GPT-4 / Claude Moore's law made compute cheap. Scaling laws turned cheap compute into intelligence.

title: 2017 — the transformer: the T in ChatGPT
text: Before it, models read text strictly one word at a time, left to right — and kept forgetting. Like watching a 500-episode serial and being asked in episode 500 what happened in episode 3. The early models simply forgot. Long sentences were hard, long documents hopeless. The 2017 idea: stop reading one by one. Let every word look at every other word at once — and learn which ones deserve attention .

title: Attention, visually
text: "The animal didn't cross the street because it was too tired." What does "it" refer to? You knew instantly. So does the model: The animal didn't cross the street because it was… strong attention — "it" means the animal weak attention to "street" — considered, rejected Change "tired" to "wide" and the thick line jumps to street . Context decides meaning. 🥚 🎵 …all you need is 🎵

title: Why this changed everything
text: Parallel, not sequential → thousands of GPUs can work at once → we could finally train on the whole internet Long memory → episode 3 is never forgotten; every word stays visible One design for everything → text, images, audio, code, proteins The paper: "Attention Is All You Need" — Vaswani et al., Google, 2017 📺 3Blue1Brown — Attention in transformers, visually explained — watch this before next week.

title: 2018 → today: the LLM era
text: 2018–19 — GPT-1, GPT-2: transformer + huge text = surprising fluency 2020 — GPT-3: scaling laws in action; size alone unlocks new abilities Nov 2022 — ChatGPT: 100 million users in two months 2023–24 — GPT-4, Claude, Gemini, open models; multimodal 2025–26 — reasoning models and agents: AI that plans and uses tools (our Week 7)

title: The whole picture 🗺️
text: 1950 Turing test 1956 "AI" named 1959 Samuel: weights ❄️ '70s winter 1980s expert systems ❄️ '80s winter 1997 Deep Blue 2012 deep learning 💥 2016 AlphaGo 2017 transformer ⚡ 2022 ChatGPT AGI? the eventual goal: machines matching humans across the board 75 years: rules → learning → deep learning → attention → …?

title: Zooming in: everything since ChatGPT 🔍
text: Nov 2022 ChatGPT 2023 GPT-4, Claude, Gemini Llama: open weights arrive Sep 2024 reasoning models "think before answering" Oct 2024 two Nobel prizes 🏅 Jan 2025 the DeepSeek moment 💥 2025–26 agents, coding assistants, models on your laptop Four years. Faster than the previous forty.

title: January 2025 — the DeepSeek moment 💥
text: A Chinese lab releases DeepSeek-R1 : a reasoning model roughly matching the best closed models — released free and open-weight , and reportedly trained for a tiny fraction of the usual cost. Nvidia's share price fell around 17% in a single day — one of the largest one-day losses in market history The assumption that only a handful of giant labs could reach the frontier broke Its reasoning was distilled into small models — frontier-style ability on a laptop Like a small regional airline suddenly flying the same route, on time, at a tenth of the fare. The big carriers' pricing stopped making sense overnight.

title: Where things stand today 🧭
text: The frontier is crowded. GPT, Claude, Gemini and Grok families leapfrog each other every few months. No single winner; pick per task. Open weights are close behind. DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi and others trail the frontier by months, not years — and you can run them yourself. Small models got good. Useful models now run on a laptop or a phone, offline and private. Cost collapsed. What cost dollars per query in 2023 costs a fraction of a rupee today. The action moved to agents. Not "answer my question" but "do this task, using these tools" — our Week 7.

title: Last week, in one chain 🔗
text: Recap examples a line weight w loss training the model inference two weights a matrix A farmer asked how much fertiliser to use. We had no rule — only examples. So we guessed a line, measured how wrong it was, and hunted for a better weight. Everything today hangs off that chain. Nothing is replaced; we only add links.

title: A real farmer has more than one dial 🌾
text: Last week we gave him fertiliser, then rainfall. A real season has far more than two things pulling on the yield: 🌾 fertiliser ☔ rainfall 🌡️ temperature 🪨 soil type 🌱 seed variety 📅 sowing date 🐛 pest pressure 🧪 pesticide 💧 watering schedule Nine things that matter → nine weights : yield = w₁×fertiliser + w₂×rain + w₃×temp + … + w₉×watering And there is still only one loss . All nine numbers have to come down together — nudge the fertiliser weight and the watering weight may need to move too.

title: Now ask the same question about words 📖
text: A farmer has nine things that matter. How many does a machine need just to know every word in the dictionary? 100,000 words (tokens) it must know × 4,096 numbers to describe each one = 410 million weights …and that is only to know what the words mean . Not one rule of grammar yet. Not one sentence written.

title: Where we stopped, deliberately
text: Last week we found the best weight by trying values — 0.5, 0.7, 0.9, 1.1 — and keeping the one with the lowest loss. That is fine for one dial. For nine it is already painful. For 410 million it is hopeless. And GPT-4 has roughly a trillion — the dictionary is barely 0.04% of it. Trying values would still be running when the sun burns out. So: how do you find a trillion numbers? Hold that question. We need two other things first — and then we spend the whole middle of today answering it. 🔖

title: You already learned a language once 📖
text: Before anything else Nobody handed you English in one piece. It came in four stages, in this order: 1. the alphabet — a fixed set of symbols 2. vocabulary — what each word means 3. grammar — how words relate to each other 4. writing a sentence of your own A machine learning language goes through exactly these four stages . Today we do one at a time — and at the end, we come back to this slide.

title: Stage 1 — the alphabet
text: Act 1 of 5 · 🔤 A fixed set of symbols. For a model, they are not letters.

title: First, chop it up ✂️
text: Step 1 of the four: the alphabet . A model does not read words — it reads tokens , a fixed set of chunks decided before training starts. "unbelievable" un believ able "Hyderabad biryani" Hyder abad bir yani Common words are one token. Rare words get broken into pieces. Roughly: 1 token ≈ ¾ of an English word .

title: Stage 1 — click to reveal
text: Checkpoint 1 of 5 A model reads text in chunks called… tokens Rare words get… broken into several tokens Roughly, one English word is about… 1⅓ tokens (1 token ≈ ¾ of a word) Telugu or Hindi need… many more tokens for the same sentence — so they cost more

title: Stage 2 — vocabulary
text: Act 2 of 5 · 📖 Knowing the symbols is not knowing what they mean.

title: Step 2: vocabulary — what each token means 🔢
text: "it" [0.21, −0.88, 0.04, …] a long list of numbers "animal" [0.19, −0.79, 0.11, …] similar meaning → similar numbers How long is that list, really? 4,096 numbers — for every single token. Exactly like Samuel turning a checkers board into four numbers — just a much longer list. These lists are called embeddings . 4,096 × 100,000 tokens — that is where the 410 million came from. 🔖

title: Meaning has a direction 🗺️
text: If a word is a list of numbers, it is a point on a map . And the journeys between points mean something. Hyderabad Telangana is the capital of → Bengaluru Karnataka is the capital of → same direction · same length · same relationship Nobody programmed "capital of". It fell out of predicting text — which means the model built a map of meaning on its own.

title: One sentence, for the rest of today 📝
text: We will use this all session "The animal didn't cross the street because it was too tired." Pretend an embedding is just two numbers instead of 4,096 — say aliveness and place-ness : alive place animal 1 0 a living thing, not a place street 0 1 a place, not alive cross 0 0 a verb — neither it 1 1 ambiguous — could be either! Hold on to these four rows. We come back to them later and do the whole calculation.

title: Real embeddings, right now
text: Live demo 🔬 projector.tensorflow.org — 10,000 real words, each one a list of 200 numbers, squashed onto a 3-D map you can spin. 1. Search a word — try river , then engineer , then a name 2. Look at its nearest neighbours 3. Ask the class: why are those the neighbours? Nobody placed those words. They landed there from reading text.

title: Two sentences. One word. Same numbers.
text: The crack in the story 🪤 "I sat on the bank of the river and watched the sunset." "I went to the bank to withdraw some cash." …the bank of the river… bank → [0.41, −0.22, 0.87, …] …the bank to withdraw cash… bank → [0.41, −0.22, 0.87, …] = Identical. Every single number. The dictionary has one entry for "bank". It has not read the sentence yet. So how does it ever tell a riverbank from a cash machine? 🤔 Vocabulary alone is not enough . A word's meaning depends on the words around it — and that is the next stage.

title: Stage 2 — click to reveal
text: Checkpoint 2 of 5 A token turned into a list of numbers is an… embedding Words with similar meanings end up… close together on the map "Hyderabad → Telangana" and "Bengaluru → Karnataka" share… the same direction — the relationship itself "bank" in two different sentences starts out… identical — the table has not read the sentence Who decided those numbers? nobody — they were learned. That is the next act.

title: Who taught you grammar? 📐
text: The question that matters Somebody did. A teacher, a textbook, a parent correcting you. Rules, written down, handed over. Nobody did that for the model. No one wrote "a pronoun refers back to a noun" anywhere inside GPT. Week 1: people spent twenty years trying to hand-write the rules. Expert systems. It failed, and the field froze twice. So before we can look at grammar, we have to answer a different question: how does it learn anything at all?

title: How does it learn anything ?
text: Act 3 of 5 · ⚙️ Nobody wrote the rules. So where did they come from? ⚠️ We leave words alone for ten minutes and go back to the farmer. Then we bring the idea straight back to language.

title: Lost on a hillside, in thick fog 🌫️
text: A story first You are somewhere on a hill at dusk. The fog is so thick you can see your own boots and nothing else. You need to get down to the valley. You cannot see the valley. You cannot see the path. You have no map. But you can feel which way the ground tilts under your feet.

title: You just invented the algorithm 🥾
text: Feel the slope. Step downhill. Feel again. Repeat until the ground is flat. high error 😖 lowest error — best weights 🎯 you are here feel the slope with your foot → step downhill repeat… and you arrive. That is gradient descent — and it is how every model in this course learns its weights.

title: You have seen this hill before 🌾
text: Last week we drew the farmer's loss for different weights. Turn it on its side and it is the same picture: weight w → loss → w = 0.55 slope says: go right w = 0.9 · loss 18 🎯 Same valley. The farmer's hill just happens to have only one direction to walk in.

title: So what is the hill, for language ? 🏔️
text: The farmer had examples: fertiliser in, yield out, and a gap we could measure. Where does a language model get its examples? a piece of real text "Chennai is famous for its ___" from a book, a website, anywhere the model guesses from those 4,096-number lists compare with what was actually written there how wrong? → loss Nobody labelled any of this. The text already contains its own answer. Same three things as the farmer: a guess, a true value, a gap. That gap is the hill.

title: Add one more weight and the hill becomes a landscape 🏞️
text: Two weights: w₁ runs one way across the floor, w₂ the other. Height is still the loss. w₁ w₂ loss (height) start: badly wrong big step …then smaller the bottom: the best pair of weights Each step is a fraction of the slope — so as the ground flattens, the steps shrink by themselves. That fraction is the learning rate. 🥾 Nothing new is being invented as this grows. It is the farmer's arithmetic, with more columns. 🌾

title: Too small, too big, just right 👣
text: too small correct — but takes for ever too big leaps the valley, climbs the far side big, then smaller 🎯 fast at first, careful at the end That step size has a name: the learning rate . It is the single most important dial in training a model. 🥚 how fast do you learn?

title: The dip that is not the valley 🕳️
text: stuck here flat underfoot — so it stops the real valley A local minimum : everywhere around you is uphill, so you stop — but you are not at the bottom. In the fog, you cannot tell the difference.

title: The bakery, and the price of a sandwich 🥪
text: You already do this 6 rupees each, 330 sold a day. Drop the price by 25 paise and 15 more people buy. How far do you go? price cuts of 25 paise → revenue → ₹1980 ₹6.00 ₹1983.75 🎯 ₹5.75 ₹1980 ₹5.50 ₹1968 ₹5.25 ₹1950 ₹5.00 One cut: better. Two cuts: back where you started — you have gone past the top. Same walk, same overshoot, no equation anywhere.

title: The coach who only sees the final score ⚽
text: A story first A goal is missed. Eleven players touched the ball. Whose fault was it? Nobody told the coach. He only knows one thing: it did not go in. So he works backwards . The striker shot wide — but the pass came late. The pass was late because the midfielder was out of position. He was out of position because the defender cleared it slowly. Every player gets a share of the blame — and the share is not equal.

title: Backwards through the team 🔁
text: defender midfield striker missed 😖 the loss blame flows backwards, share by share nudge 0.01 nudge 0.08 nudge 0.30 That is backpropagation : one number at the end, turned into a personal correction for every weight in the network.

title: So what does "downhill" mean with a trillion dials? 🧭
text: 1 weight a curve downhill = left, or right 2 weights a landscape downhill = a compass direction a trillion weights w₁ → +0.004 w₂ → −0.031 w₃ → +0.000 … a trillion more you cannot draw it downhill = one nudge per weight And that list is exactly what the coach just worked out — every weight's share of the blame. Backpropagation finds the list. Gradient descent takes the step. Same move, twice named.

title: The man who built it in 1958 🧠
text: The people Frank Rosenblatt builds the Perceptron — a machine that learns from examples by nudging weights. Exactly what we just described. The New York Times reports it will soon walk, talk, see, write, reproduce itself and be conscious of its existence. In 1969 a book proves what a single perceptron cannot do. Funding stops. The field freezes. Rosenblatt dies in 1971, aged 43. He was not wrong. He was fifty years early — the idea needed data and computers that would not exist until 2012.

title: From one weight to a trillion 📈
text: The fog walk does not care how many weights there are. One step adjusts all of them at once. the farmer 1 weight AlexNet, 2012 60 million GPT-3, 2020 175 billion today ~1 trillion Same walk. Same slope. Just a hill with a trillion directions.

title: The farmer, one thousand times wider 🌾
text: Week 1: two inputs, two weights, one multiply-and-add. the farmer [40 12] × [0.6] [1.2] = 38.4 one word inside GPT [0.21 −0.88 … 4,096 numbers] × [ 4,096 × 4,096 weights ] identical arithmetic — multiply, add, repeat There is no new maths in here. There is just an enormous amount of the same maths .

title: Why it needs a GPU 🎮
text: One brilliant professor doing seventeen million sums, one after another — versus a thousand ordinary students doing seventeen thousand each, all at the same time. The students finish first. Every time. A CPU is the professor: a few very clever cores. A GPU is the classroom: thousands of simple cores doing identical arithmetic in parallel. Built for video-game graphics. It turned out that shading a million pixels and running a neural network are the same shape of problem .

title: How it learns — click to reveal
text: Checkpoint 3 of 5 Walking downhill in the fog is called… gradient descent The slope under your foot tells you… which way reduces the loss The size of each step is called the… learning rate Too big a step means… you overshoot the valley and training blows up A dip that is not the real bottom is a… local minimum Working backwards from one mistake to every weight's share of the blame is… backpropagation Backpropagation happens… only during training — never while it is answering you GPUs beat CPUs here because… thousands of identical sums run in parallel

title: Stage 3 — grammar
text: Act 4 of 5 · 📐 The rules it was never given. This is attention.

title: Five hundred people, and you hear your name 🎉
text: A story first A wedding hall. Deafening. Music, a hundred conversations, children running. You have stopped even trying to listen. Then someone across the room says your name . You hear it instantly — and you have no idea what anyone else said. Your brain scored every sound in that hall for relevance to you, and spent almost all of its attention on one. That is the entire idea, and it has a name.

title: Remember this sentence? 🐘
text: "The animal didn't cross the street because it was too tired." The animal didn't cross the street because it was… "it" pays attention to "animal" Last week I showed you this line and said "the model knows". Today: how.

title: Step 1: every word asks, and advertises 🙋
text: Query (Q) "what am I looking for?" "it" asks: which noun could I be referring to? Key (K) "what do I offer?" "animal" advertises: I am a living noun Value (V) "what do I contribute?" the actual meaning passed along if chosen A marriage bureau. The Query is what a family is looking for. The Key is the one-line summary on each profile. The Value is the actual person behind the profile. Match queries against keys — then you get the values.

title: Step 2: remember our sentence? 🔢
text: "The animal didn't cross the street because it was too tired." alive place animal 1 0 street 0 1 cross 0 0 it [ 1 1 ] still ambiguous We are about to fix that 1 1 — by hand, with three multiplications.

title: Step 3: build the Query for "it" ✖️
text: Multiply "it"'s embedding by W Q — a learned weight matrix, found by the fog walk in the last act: "it" [ 1 1 ] × W_Q (learned) [ 2 0 ] [ 0 0.5 ] = the Query [ 2 0.5 ] 1×2 + 1×0 = 2 · 1×0 + 1×0.5 = 0.5 "I am mostly looking for something ALIVE, and a little for a PLACE."

title: But where did W Q come from? 🎲→🎯
text: It started as random numbers . Watch the same sentence with an untrained W Q : DAY ONE — W_Q is random [ 1 1 ] × [ 0.3 0.9 ] [ 0.7 0.2 ] = [ 1.0 1.1 ] animal 40% street 45% ← wrong! ↓ the sentence said "tired". Streets do not get tired. LOSS is high. ↓ backpropagation: nudge all four numbers in W_Q a little ↓ repeat, over millions of sentences MONTHS LATER [ 2 0 ] [ 0 0.5 ] animal 74% ✓

title: Step 4: score the Query against every Key 🎯
text: Multiply matching positions, add them up. That is all a "score" is: Query [ 2 0.5 ] · Key animal [ 1 0 ] 2×1 + 0.5×0 = 2.0 street [ 0 1 ] 2×0 + 0.5×1 = 0.5 cross [ 0 0 ] 2×0 + 0.5×0 = 0.0 animal wins — because it is the only thing in the sentence that is alive

title: Step 5: scores become percentages 📊
text: Raw scores are hard to compare. Turn them into shares that add to 100%: animal 2.0 74% street 0.5 16% cross 0.0 10% grow each score: e² = 7.39 e⁰·⁵ = 1.65 e⁰ = 1.00 share of the total (10.04): 7.39/10.04 = 74% adds up to 100%

title: And now watch "it" move 🎬
text: Mix the Values in those proportions — 74% animal, 16% street, 10% cross: 0.74 × [1 0] + 0.16 × [0 1] + 0.10 × [0 0] "it" before [ 1.00 1.00 ] alive? maybe. place? maybe. "it" after [ 0.74 0.16 ] alive. mostly, clearly, alive. The word "it" has literally been rewritten to mean the animal.

title: Step 6: many heads, many layers 🧅
text: That whole process runs many times over, in parallel — each copy watching for something different. head 1 who does "it" mean? head 2 grammar, verb tense head 3 who did what to whom …and more 96 of them …then the whole thing repeats, layer after layer early layers: grammar · middle: meaning · late: what comes next That is a transformer. Everything else is engineering detail.

title: Stage 3 — click to reveal
text: Checkpoint 4 of 5 Hearing your name across a noisy hall is an everyday version of… attention Q, K and V stand for… Query, Key, Value The Query is… what this word is looking for Attention scores are turned into… percentages that add up to 100% Q, K and V are produced by… three sets of weights, learned by walking downhill

title: Stage 4 — writing a sentence
text: Act 5 of 5 · ✍️ Four stages down. This is what it all builds to.

title: What is ChatGPT actually doing when…
text: What is ChatGPT actually doing when it answers you? Guess before the next slide. Is it looking things up? Thinking? Something else?

title: It is guessing the next word. That's it.
text: "Chennai is famous for its ___" beaches 31% filter coffee 24% Marina 18% heat 12% …thousands more Pick one → add it to the sentence → ask again. Loop. Every essay, poem and program it writes comes out of this one loop.

title: Training and inference, at real scale ⚖️
text: TRAINING the fog walk, billions of steps months · tens of thousands of GPUs happens ONCE · costs millions INFERENCE one pass through the weights under a second happens EVERY time you type · costs cents This is why a model has a knowledge cut-off — and why correcting ChatGPT never teaches it anything.

title: From "next word" to something helpful 🎓
text: PRETRAINING read the internet, guess the next word FINE-TUNING shown good examples of helpful answers RLHF humans rank answers; it learns what we prefer raw next-word machine → the assistant you actually talk to A pretrained model is brilliant and unusable. The last two steps are what make it polite, helpful and safe enough to ship .

title: Stage 4 — click to reveal
text: Checkpoint 5 of 5 An LLM generates text by… predicting the next token, over and over Training happens once; inference happens… every single time you send a message Correcting ChatGPT in a chat changes the weights… never — it only lives in that conversation Humans ranking answers to teach preferences is called… RLHF

text: The map, completed how YOU learned how a MODEL learned 1. the alphabet → tokens — a fixed vocabulary of chunks 2. vocabulary → embeddings — meaning as coordinates 3. grammar → attention — Q, K and V 4. writing a sentence → predicting the next token, again and again One difference, and it is the whole course: you were taught. It was not. It found all four by walking downhill.

title: 🔧 Three small fixes that make it exactly right
text: Your Week 2 work Not mistakes to be embarrassed about. Each one is a common trap, and fixing it deepens the idea. 1 · "The volume needs to be around 14" If you already knew the answer was 14, you'd just jump straight there. 🤔 ✓ Gradient descent never knows the answer . The measure only says "too loud, and roughly how much" . The direction, not the destination. 2 · "2 spoons, then 1 spoon" That halves the amount in one go, and it treats the spoons as the measure. ✓ The measure is how far off the taste is (the loss). The step is a small nudge: "a bit strong, a little less next time." 3 · "Too much chemical harms the crop; too little doesn't work" A brilliant real-world example! It describes the goal , but not yet the method . ✓ Add the loop: spray a dose → check the pests and the crop → adjust a little → repeat . Finding the balance by repeated small corrections is gradient descent. 🌫️ Still fuzzy for a few of you: "how do the scores turn into percentages, and then into the final numbers?" Fair. Today we redo it slowly with toy numbers, on the "Inside the model" slide (step 6). And remember: you only need the idea , not the arithmetic.

title: 💬 Two questions worth answering for everyone
text: You asked me privately "How much maths should I learn, versus building projects?" Aim for intuition, not derivations . Know what each idea does : 📉 gradient → which way is downhill 🎲 probability → the odds for the next word 📐 vectors → meaning as a position That's all this course needs. Build first ; learn deeper maths when a project actually needs it. It sticks far better that way. "I understand the examples, but where do I use them?" A great question. Here's where each one shows up: 🔤 Tokens → why chats have limits and API bills (Week 5) 🗺️ Embeddings → how AI searches your own documents (Week 6) 👀 Attention → why the words in your prompt matter ( today ) 📉 Gradient descent → how every model you use was trained Keep asking. Every private question makes the next class better for everyone. 🙌

text: 1 of 4 · tokens Not letters. Not words. Chunks the model was built around. "unbelievable" un believ able 3 tokens, 1 word Three consequences you will meet today : 💰 You are billed per token — a longer prompt literally costs more 📏 The context window is measured in tokens — that is the "it forgot" ceiling ⚖️ Telugu and Hindi burn far more tokens than English for the same sentence All three come back within the hour.

text: 2 of 4 · embeddings Every piece of text becomes a long list of numbers — and things that mean similar things land near each other. idli dosa biryani algebra calculus food lives here maths lives over there Why you care "Find me the bit of this document that ANSWERS this" = find the nearest point Week 6: RAG AI over your own data If only one Week 2 idea survives to Week 8, let it be this one.

title: Training is over. You are talking to a finished thing ❄️
text: 3 of 4 · frozen TRAINING · once months · thousands of GPUs the fog walk, a trillion times over weights change this already happened, without you INFERENCE · every time you type a second · weights completely frozen nothing it learns here is kept only your PROMPT changes ← which is the only lever you hold Three things follow: the model's own knowledge stops on the day training ended (chat apps patch this by searching the web and pasting the results in), it does not remember you between chats, and prompting is the entire steering wheel. That last one is today.

title: It is predicting, not knowing 🎲
text: 4 of 4 · prediction One token at a time, always: "what comes next?" — then it reads its own answer back and asks again. The capital of Telangana is Hyderabad (91%) Secunderabad (4%) … (5%) Nothing in there checks whether the answer is true . It checks whether it is likely . Which is exactly why it is most dangerous when it sounds most confident — and why Act 4 exists.

title: 🔍 Inside the Model: How One Next Token Gets Picked
text: Deeper · how one token is chosen Toy numbers so we can follow along. Real models use the same steps with much bigger tables. 1 Your text "I spread butter on my ___" I spread butter on my Split into tokens (Week 2) ➜ 🧠 THE MODEL 2 Look up each token's embedding I spread butter on my 🍽️ food 0.0 +0.4 +1.6 0.0 0.0 🧍 body +0.3 +0.3 0.0 0.0 +0.4 ✋ action 0.0 +1.4 0.0 +0.2 0.0 🔗 link-word +0.9 0.0 0.0 +1.1 +1.0 Each token = a column of d numbers (here d = 4; real models: thousands). Like a word's profile scores . Real dimensions have no names; we labelled ours to make it readable. 3 Attention: tokens look at each other W q Query "What am I looking for?" W k Key "What do I have to offer?" W v Value "What info do I pass on?" "my" listens to: I 5% spread 15% butter 55% on 10% my 15% ↻ repeated in many stacked layers ➜ 4 "my" now +1.3 +0.2 +0.4 +0.3 Context vector : "my", now soaked in meaning from "butter" & "spread" ⤵ 5 Compare with every word in the vocabulary context +1.3 +0.2 +0.4 +0.3 × 🍽️ 🧍 ✋ 🔗 score toast +2.0 0.0 +0.2 0.0 +2.7 bread +1.8 0.0 0.0 0.0 +2.3 hands +0.5 +1.3 +0.3 0.0 +1.0 face 0.0 +2.0 0.0 0.0 +0.4 arms 0.0 +1.8 0.0 0.0 +0.4 … and ~100,000 more words Multiply-and-add = a match score . High score → "this word fits what comes next." ➜ 6 Scores → probabilities toast 48% bread 34% hands 9% face 5% arms 5% All add up to 100% ➜ 7 Pick toast Add it to the text, then do it all again for the next token ↻

title: 🔁 Every New Token Goes Back Into the Input
text: Deeper · the loop The model never writes a whole sentence at once. It predicts one token, adds it to the text, and reads everything again. 📝 Input the model reads yellow = what the model is paying most attention to ➜ 🧠 Model predict next token ➜ Top guesses ➜ Pick … ↩ the pick is added to the end of the input ▶ Next token ⏩ Play all 🎲 Replay with a surprise first pick ⟲ Reset

title: 🔄 Change One Word, Change the Prediction
text: Deeper · context The last word is "my" both times. What's around it decides what comes next. How much "my" listens to each word: I 5% spread 15% butter 55% on 10% my 15% ➜ "my" now +1.3 +0.2 +0.4 +0.3 ➜ toast 48% bread 34% hands 9% face 5% arms 5% ➜ toast How much "my" listens to each word: I 5% spread 15% sunscreen 55% on 10% my 15% ➜ "my" now -0.1 +1.3 +0.4 +0.3 ➜ face 43% arms 33% hands 19% toast 3% bread 3% ➜ face Why? Attention let "my" pull in meaning from the thing being spread. "butter" makes the vector point toward food ; "sunscreen" flips it toward body . Different vector → different match scores → different next word. That's what "context" means: every earlier token can change the guess. It's also why a better prompt gets a better answer. ✋ Your turn: "I spread the news to my ___" — type your guess in chat, then tap. 👥 friends / family . One new word changed what "spread" itself means: not smearing any more, but telling. Attention lets "news" rewrite "spread", and the rewritten meaning points to people, not bread.

title: 🎂 The Big Picture: AI Is a Five-Layer Cake

Each layer only works if the one below it does. No power → no chips running → no data centre → no model → no app. Where the money shows up Huang's point: the lower layers are a huge build-out, but real value is created at the top — when applications solve someone's problem. ⭐ You are here this week Week 2 opened layer 4 (how models think). title: 🗺️ From Raw Data to Your Screen: The AI Lifecycle
text: Big picture · 2 of 2 The cake showed what AI runs on . This shows what happens to a model — built once, then served, extended and used. 1 · Training Building the brain (once, very expensive) Data collection web, books, code, licensed data Data curation clean, de-duplicate, filter harmful/low-quality Tokenization turn text into tokens (Week 2) Pre-training predict the next token, trillions of times Post-training fine-tuning, RLHF — teach it to be helpful & safe Evaluation benchmarks, red-teaming before release 🎓 Chef goes to culinary school Week 2 ➜ 2 · Inference Running the brain (every single question) Serving engines vLLM, TensorRT-LLM — run models fast Batching answer many users on one GPU at once Caching KV cache & prompt caching — don't redo work GPU memory management fit long conversations in limited memory Context management what fits in the context window, what gets trimmed Sampling settings how adventurous the next-word pick is 🍳 Chef cooking orders during dinner rush Weeks 2 & 5 ➜ 3 · Agents Giving the brain hands and a to-do list Custom harness the loop: think → act → check → repeat Tools & connectors search, files, email, calendar (MCP) Skills packaged know-how for specific tasks Long-term memory remembers you across conversations Retrieval (RAG) look things up in your own documents Automation & guardrails scheduled workflows, safety checks 👨‍🍳 Head chef with a team, a phone and a shopping list Weeks 6 & 7 ➜ 4 · Applications What people actually use it for Writing essays, reports, email drafting Summarizing papers, meetings, long documents Code generation write, explain and debug code Math & reasoning step-by-step problem solving Research & analysis literature scans, data questions Tutoring, translation, support chatbots for real people 🍽️ The dishes on the menu Weeks 3 & 4 · ⭐ today 💡 Prompting (today) works at every stage after training: it shapes inference, steers agents, and decides how good your application's output is.

title: 🧠 + 🧩 The Model Guesses the Next Token. The Harness Does the Rest.
text: Big picture · model vs harness What you call "ChatGPT" or "Claude" is two things working together: a model and the harness around it. Inside the model: It's 31°C and rainy → ? guess one token → add it → guess again… until "stop" 🧠 The Model (inference) a brilliant autocomplete Takes text in, predicts the next token Repeats that very fast (dozens of tokens a second) ✗ Can't browse, run code, or send email ✗ Remembers nothing between calls (the harness resends the chat) ✗ Doesn't decide what happens next 🧩 The Harness (agent program) ordinary software wrapped around the model Packs the prompt: instructions + chat history + list of tools Collects tokens into words, then reads the result Decides: is this a final answer, or a request to use a tool? Runs the tool (search, calculator, calendar) and feeds the result back Loops until done, and adds memory, limits and safety checks 1 · You "What's the weather in Chennai?" 2 · Harness Adds instructions + tool list, sends to model 3 · Model Writes, token by token: get_weather("Chennai") 4 · Harness Spots a tool call, runs it → 31°C, rain 5 · Model Reads the result, writes: "It's 31°C and rainy…" 6 · Harness Sees a final answer → shows it to you 💡 Myth: "ChatGPT searched the web." Reality: the model wrote a request to search; the harness did the searching.

title: Solid ground ✅
text: Checkpoint 1 Type your answer in chat — do NOT press send 2 I count 3 · 2 · 1 3 Everyone sends together The context window is measured in… tokens — that is the "it forgot" ceiling "idli" sits near "dosa" because… meaning is a position, and it was learned — nobody placed them Does the model learn from our chat? No. Frozen weights. It re-reads the chat every time — that is context, not learning It optimises for… plausible, not true Attention, in one sentence, is… words are rewritten by the words around them ("butter" turned "my" into something food-ish) That is the foundation. Everything else today is skill , not theory.

title: Tomorrow, a new classmate joins your project group 👩‍🎓
text: The session proper She has read every book, paper and website ever written. She is the most widely-read person you will ever meet, and she is on your team. She also has three peculiarities: She has never met you and knows nothing about your project She forgets everything the moment she leaves the room She will never say "I don't understand" — she will guess, confidently How do you explain the task to her? That question is the whole of today.

title: You already do this. Every day. 🛺
text: You get into an auto and say: "Anna, temple." Or you say: "Birla Mandir — the Khairatabad side gate, not the main one. It shuts at nine, so the flyover if traffic is bad. How much?" The second driver is not smarter. The brief is better. Destination · landmark · constraint · format of the answer. You did all four without thinking.

title: Five things a good brief has
text: Act 1 · the brief WHO who should it be? "you are a careers adviser…" WHY the situation "I am a final-year ECE student…" WHAT the actual task "rewrite this paragraph…" HOW shape of the answer "120 words, plain English, no bullets" SHOW an example "like this one: …" WHO · WHY · WHAT · HOW · SHOW You will not use all five every time. Most bad prompts are missing three of them. The auto driver got WHY, WHAT and HOW — and that was the whole difference.

title: Same question. Same model. 🔄
text: Before / after ✗ "Write a cover letter for a job." → generic, could be anyone, mentions "passionate" four times ✓ "You are a careers adviser who has placed many engineering graduates. I am a final-year ECE student in Hyderabad applying for a semiconductor design internship. My only relevant experience is a college project on chip floor-planning. Write a cover letter of about 150 words. Plain English, no clichés, and do not use the word 'passionate'. Show me two versions with different opening lines." Nothing clever happened. Someone just said what they wanted.

title: Sixteen people, one prompt
text: Everyone, together 🙋 1. Open your chatbot. Send exactly: "Give me tips to study better." 2. Paste the first line of what you got into chat — hold it, we send on three 3. Now rewrite it using WHO · WHY · WHAT · HOW for your actual subject and situation 4. Paste the first line of the new one. Same countdown. Two rounds, same room, same tools. Look at the difference between round one and round two.

title: The brief ✅
text: Checkpoint 1 of 3 1 Type in chat — do NOT press send 2 I count 3 · 2 · 1 3 Send together The five parts of a brief are WHO, WHY, WHAT, HOW and… SHOW Sixteen vague prompts gave sixteen similar answers because… a vague prompt collapses onto the most average answer in the training data "Do not use the word passionate" is an example of a… constraint — negative ones work too

title: Move 1: show , don't describe 📋
text: Act 2 · two power moves Describing the style you want is hard. Showing two examples is easy — and works better. describing it "Summarise each paper in a short, punchy, not-too-formal way that highlights the main finding." → it guesses what you mean by "punchy" showing it Paper: Smith 2019 → "Sleep loss hits memory harder than mood." Paper: Rao 2021 → "Cheap sensors can spot crop disease a week early." Paper: [yours] → Two examples and it has the pattern. The jargon for this is few-shot prompting — and you have been doing it since school.

title: Move 2: give it room to think 🧠
text: Add five words — "think step by step" — and hard questions get noticeably better answers. This sounds like superstition. It is not. straight to the answer the first token it writes must already BE the answer "think step by step" it writes the working first — and then reads its own working Remember: every token it writes becomes part of what it reads next. So the working is not decoration. The working is the thinking.

title: The power moves ✅
text: Checkpoint 2 of 3 1 Type in chat — do NOT press send 2 I count 3 · 2 · 1 3 Send together Giving two examples instead of describing a style is called… few-shot prompting "Think step by step" works because… each token it writes becomes input for the next — the working is the thinking If your examples contain a mistake, the model will… copy it, confidently. Your examples are the specification

title: Don't start over. Steer. 🎯
text: Act 3 · when it comes back wrong The most common mistake: a bad answer arrives, and people delete everything and rewrite the prompt from scratch. The whole conversation is re-read every single time. So a correction is added information , not a fresh start: "Too formal. Same content, how you'd explain it to a friend." "The second point is wrong — students here don't pay that fee. Redo it without that." "Good. Now cut it to half the length and keep the example." Three rounds of steering beats one perfect prompt — and it is far less work.

title: Fix this prompt, one addition each
text: Relay 🙋 "Explain machine learning." 1. In chat, add exactly one thing that would improve it — a WHO, a WHY, a HOW, a constraint 2. One line each. Do not repeat what someone above you wrote 3. I will stitch them together and we will run the result live Sixteen small additions make a prompt none of us would have written alone.

title: 🧪 Two quick experiments first. Explanations after.
text: Act 4 · the dials, and the edges Watch, guess what's going on, type your theory in chat. No wrong answers yet. Experiment 1 · Same prompt, one hidden dial "Write a one-line tagline for a filter-coffee café in Chennai." ▶ Dial at 0 · run 3× ▶ Dial at 1 · run 3× Experiment 2 · Ask about something that doesn't exist 📚 "List 3 research papers (authors, year, journal) on using AI to predict paddy yield in Andhra Pradesh." 🧑‍🔬 "What did Dr. K. Aravind's 2019 paper on monsoon prediction find, and which journal published it?" 📼 recorded examples ⚙️ live mode Save

title: Two consequences you will feel every day
text: Act 4 · the dials, and the edges Creativity is a dial. Always pick the top word → dull and repetitive. Sometimes pick a lower one → surprising and creative. That dial has a name: temperature . Hallucination is not a bug in the usual sense. The model optimises for plausible-sounding , not for true . A confident wrong citation is the system working exactly as built. One of these you can turn. The other you have to guard against — and that is the rest of this act. 🥚 the dial has a name

title: 🌡️ Temperature: how bold is the pick?
text: The dial · how it works Every option below means the same thing . Temperature only decides how boldly the harness rolls the dice between them. (Nothing to do with weather: the name is borrowed from physics, where hotter = more random.) "Thank you so much for your ___" odds for the next token T = 1.0 0 · always the top word 1 · the model's own odds 2 · wild 🎲 Roll the dice 20 times at this temperature ✍️ Let it write the whole sentence ×3 one token at a time, same dial Each word's colour = how likely it was: likely less likely long shot 🎲 Roll 20× ✍️ Write 3 sentences T = 0 T = 1 T = 2 ⟲ Clear

title: 🎛️ Turn the dial on a real model
text: The dial · live Pick a prompt, set the temperature, run it three times . Do the three answers agree? Prompt Temperature T = 1.0 0 0.5 1.0 ▶ Run 3 times 📼 recorded ⚙️ Live mode setup your key stays in this browser only — never in the slides or the repo Save Forget key

title: 🙈 ChatGPT and Claude have no dial. Or do they?
text: The dial · where is it? The dial is still there. It's just not yours to turn in the chat app. 1 · It's hidden, not gone The company sets the temperature for you, inside the harness . You can't see the number or change it. Why hide it? Most people would set it wrong, and one sensible default works for most chats. Where the dial is visible: 🔗 Google AI Studio (free · slider on the right) 🔗 Claude Workbench (pick Haiku 4.5 , then model settings) 🔗 OpenAI Playground (pick GPT-4.1 ) ⚠️ The newest models (Claude Sonnet 5, Opus 5, GPT-5) have removed the dial . The makers' advice: steer with your prompt instead. 👉 card 3 2 · Myth: "set your temperature to 0" Typing that into ChatGPT does not touch the dial . The model only writes tokens; the dial lives in the harness, out of its reach. It may still act calmer. That's not the dial moving. Your words changed the context, and the context changed the odds. 🔄 Regenerate / Retry = the same prompt, a fresh roll of the dice. 3 · What you can do: move the odds with words Narrow the answer (like turning it down): "Give the single most common…" · "Answer in one word" · "Use exactly this format:" · "Only use the text I pasted" Widen the answer (like turning it up): "Give 10 unusual…" · "Avoid the obvious ideas" · "Surprise me" · "Three very different options" 💡 The dial reshapes the odds you already have. Your prompt decides what the odds are in the first place. Next slide: proof.

title: 🗣️ Same dial. Different words.
text: The dial · your words Temperature locked at T = 1.0 for all three. Only the prompt changes. Each runs 3 times. ▶ Run all three 📼 recorded Live mode uses the key from the previous slide. Same model, same dial, same randomness. The words decided how much the answers could vary. That's prompting.

title: 🙋 "If the dial is disappearing, why learn it?"
text: The dial · your questions Because the dice never went away 🎲 Every answer is still one roll from a set of odds . Only the knob was removed; the company now picks the setting. 🔄 It explains things you see every day: why the same prompt gives different answers , and why Regenerate works. ✅ It gives you a free check: ask twice . If the two answers disagree on a fact, the model wasn't sure. Verify it. 🛠️ Plenty of tools still have the knob: Google's Gemini, cheaper Claude and GPT models, and open models you can run yourself. You'll set it in code in Week 5 . When to turn it down, when to turn it up 🧊 Low 0 – 0.3 Facts, maths, code, extracting data, filling a fixed format, grading or classifying. Anything you want the same every time . 🙂 Middle 0.5 – 1 Everyday writing: emails, summaries, explanations. Sounds natural, not robotic. 🔥 High 1 + Brainstorming: names, taglines, story ideas, "10 different angles". You pick the best afterwards. ⚠️ Low is not "more correct". It is more repeatable . A wrong answer at T = 0 is wrong every single time.

title: 🎭 "Be formal" / "be poetic": is that temperature?
text: The dial · your questions No. Style words change which words are likely. Temperature changes how boldly we pick among them. Watch "Thank you so much for your ___": Plain no style asked help 45% support 25% kindness 12% guidance 9% patience 5% "Be formal" the odds move to formal words assistance 40% guidance 28% support 15% counsel 9% help 5% "Be poetic" the odds move to poetic words kindness 30% light 24% grace 20% warmth 14% help 2% Plain, T = 2 same words, flatter odds help 29% support 22% kindness 15% guidance 13% patience 10% 🧭 Your prompt = the direction Formal, poetic, apologetic, authoritative, simple, like a lawyer… all move the odds to a different set of words . 🎲 Temperature = the spread Keeps the same words but makes the roll safer or bolder . "Be poetic" at T = 0 gives the same poetic line every time. 🤏 Closest thing to a dial in words Up: "surprise me", "avoid the obvious", "10 very different ideas". Down: "only the single best answer", "exactly this format".

title: 🎚️ Temperature only changes the spread
text: The dial · spread Same dial, two very different situations. Drag it and watch what happens to each. T = 1.0 0 0.3 1 2 🎲 Roll 10× each 🏆 Clear winner "Thank you so much for your ___" 🎲 10 rolls 🤷 Close race "Dr. K. Aravind's 2019 monsoon paper was published in ___" 🎲 10 rolls

title: 🎭 Close race + confident voice = hallucination
text: The dial · and hallucination 1 · The odds From training. A close race means the model never really learned the answer. ➜ 2 · Temperature Squeezes or stretches the spread . Adds no knowledge. ➜ 3 · The dice Roll every token , not just ties. (At T = 0: just take the top.) ➜ 4 · The sentence "…published in Nature ." No trace of the 24%. Sounds exactly like a fact. Common mix-ups, straightened out ✗ Temperature settles the close race. ✓ It only reshapes it. Low T just commits to a guess, the same one every time. ✗ The dice only come in when tokens tie. ✓ The dice run on every token (unless T = 0). ✗ The dice cause hallucination. ✓ The odds are the problem. The dice only pick which wrong answer you get. ✗ T = 0 prevents hallucination. ✓ It makes it repeatable. And some wrong answers are the model's clear favourite . What you can do about it (with words) 🔁 Ask twice. Different answers = a close race = the model is guessing. 📄 Give it the source ("use only this text"), so the odds come from facts you supplied (Week 6). 🚪 Allow an exit: "If you are not sure, say so." 🔍 Verify anything that matters (all of Week 4).

title: Where these tools genuinely fail ⚠️
text: Recent news, when it isn't searching. The model's own knowledge stops at its training date. Apps fill the gap with web search, but only when they decide to search. No sources shown? It may be out of date, and it won't say so. Exact recall. Citations, page numbers, quotes, links — plausible shapes, invented contents. Counting and careful arithmetic. It is predicting digits, not calculating. Ask for the working, or use a calculator. Your private world. Your college rules, your notes, your company's data. It has never seen any of it — that is Week 6. Knowing that it does not know. The failure underneath all the others.

title: The conversation gets full 📏
text: Everything is re-read every turn — so a long thread is not just long, it is expensive and blurry. short, focused thread sharp answers forty turns, three topics drifts, forgets, contradicts past the window the beginning silently falls off One chat, one job. New task → new chat. And if it has gone badly wrong twice, start fresh and paste in only the good parts.

title: And it needn't be words at all 🖼️🎵
text: Break anything into small pieces, number them, and predict the next piece: text → word pieces images → patches audio → sound chunks same machinery → one model, many senses Which means everything you learned today about briefing applies to a photo of your handwritten notes just as much as to text.

title: The edges ✅
text: Checkpoint 3 of 3 1 Type in chat — do NOT press send 2 I count 3 · 2 · 1 3 Send together A confident, well-formatted, completely invented citation is… the system working exactly as designed — plausible, not true A forty-turn chat about three different topics gives worse answers because… the whole thread is re-read every turn; it drifts, and eventually the start silently falls out of the window It cannot answer questions about your college's own rules because… it has never seen them. That is what Week 6 fixes Knowing where a tool stops working is most of knowing how to use it.

title: 🙏 Thank you. Real tasks, real prompts.
text: Your Week 3 work 4 real tasks, each with a bad prompt and a good one 4 / 4 easter eggs correct: temperature 🥚 4 / 4 told me honestly whether they used AI 🎂 Gradient descent, explained for me "I am a final-year CSE-AIML student and a beginner… use an everyday example… two short paragraphs… end with one summary sentence." ⭐ WHO, WHY, WHAT and HOW in one prompt, and the reflection named exactly why it worked. 💻 JavaScript, at my level "I am a B.Tech IT student and a beginner… simple English with small examples." ⭐ One line of WHO + HOW turned a dictionary definition into "an answer suited to my level". 🎛️ The dial, tested "Temperature mainly affects the variety of responses rather than changing the correct answer to a straightforward maths problem." ⭐ That's the whole Week 3 lesson in one sentence. 🔧 One small fix If you ask for everything , a complete, detailed answer, you may get a very long one that's hard to read and harder to remember. Keep your WHO and WHY, then narrow the WHAT: "the main stages, one line each, with one example from my field". You can always ask for more. 🎣 One stretch try: "how many letters repeat in strawberry ?" The model said "r, 3 times"… and it was right . Checking works both ways: sometimes the check proves the AI correct. 📝 Haven't sent yours yet? The form is still open. Late is much better than never.

title: 💬 Your three questions, answered
text: You asked me privately "Why do ChatGPT and Google AI Studio give different answers to the same question?" All three of your guesses are right: 🧠 Different models , trained on different data → different odds for the next word 📋 Different hidden instructions and tools (web search on or off) 🎲 Different settings , like temperature Like two good doctors from different colleges: both reasonable, not identical. "Same tool, different answer every time. Which one is best?" Why: at every word the model gives odds , and the app rolls the dice . One different pick early on, and the rest of the answer takes a different road. 🛣️ 🎲 Same temperature = same dice, not the same roll. Every run is a fresh throw. 🎯 The dice only matter when the odds are close . Sure → same answer. Unsure → it changes. ✍️ Wording, ideas: pick the one that fits you. Variety is a feature. 📌 Facts, numbers: if runs disagree , the model was guessing. Check a real source. "How do I apply what I've learned in the real world?" Start this week, three small habits: ✍️ Use WHO · WHY · WHAT · HOW · SHOW on one real assignment 🔍 Check one citation before you use it (today's 60-second check) 📒 Save one prompt you keep retyping as a skill 🚀 And the big one: your capstone , a real tool for a real person. It launches today. Keep asking. Every private question makes the next class better for everyone. 🙌

title: Easter egg
text: 🥚 This week's easter egg Out of billions of pages, a search box shows you ten. Deep Research and NotebookLM use the same trick to decide what to read before they answer you. What is the name of the field of computer science that does this? The answer is somewhere in today's session. Bring it next week, and save its first letter.

title: Who is in control? 🧠 🤖
text: From your answers last week 💡 thinking ✅ You control the AI Your head, its hands. You decide what to ask, check what comes back, and choose what to keep. AI does the heavy lifting: drafting, searching, summarising. You can explain every line of your work. 📋 copy 📋 paste ⚠️ The AI controls you Its head, your hands. It decides the answer; you just copy, paste and submit. You accept what it says without checking. Ask you a question about "your" work, and you're stuck. Same tool, same prompt box. The only difference is who is doing the thinking. Lend it your hands, never your head.

title: A letter arrives in Cambridge ✉️
text: 16 January 1913 Srinivasa Ramanujan Srinivasa Ramanujan, 1887–1920 A 25-year-old clerk at the Madras Port Trust , born in Erode, raised in Kumbakonam, writes to a famous mathematician: G. H. Hardy . Nine pages. Dozens of results. Formulas nobody had ever seen. No proofs. Just the answers.

title: Brilliant? Or a fraud? 🤔
text: What Hardy did First instinct: suspicion. Some formulas "seemed scarcely possible to believe." So he checked. He and his colleague Littlewood worked through them, one by one. Many were astonishing and new. Hardy: they "must be true, because, if they were not true, no one would have the imagination to invent them." And some were wrong. Others had already been discovered by someone else. Hardy invited him to Cambridge. Together they did some of the finest mathematics of the century: intuition, plus checking.

title: An LLM is Ramanujan without a Hardy
text: The lesson ✨ Like Ramanujan Brilliant, fast, confident. Gives you answers with no proof attached . Mostly right. Sometimes wrong, in exactly the same tone. 🔍 Your job: be Hardy Don't throw the answer away. Don't accept it blindly. Check it. That habit is today's whole session. Be Ramanujan in your ideas. Be Hardy in your checking.

title: Watch it invent, live 🎲
text: Live demo 🖥️ · Ramanujan without a Hardy 🦙 Small model (laptop) ✳️ Claude Quiz-app rule: "never say I don't know" T = 1 T = 0 ⚙️ Small model (Ollama) Claude key Claude model Save Forget key ▶ Ask 4 times Pick a question, then ask it four times.

title: First question: where did this answer come from?
text: Act 1 · checking 🧠 From memory A plain chat, no sources shown. Straight from frozen training. Great for explaining. Never trust it for facts, numbers or citations. 🌐 From a web search "Searched the web", Deep Research. Links shown. Better: you can check. But a real link can still not say what the AI claims. 📄 From your documents You uploaded the PDF (NotebookLM, a Claude Project). Best: it quotes your source. Still click the quote and read it. The further right, the easier to check. Easier to check is not the same as correct.

title: Check any citation in 60 seconds ⏱️
text: Your new habit 1 · Does it exist? Paste the exact title in quotes into Google Scholar. No hit = stop, it's probably invented. 2 · Right people, place, time? Do the authors work in that field? Did the journal exist that year? Does the year fit? 3 · Does it say that? Open it. Use Ctrl + F to find the claim. A real paper that doesn't support the sentence is still a wrong citation. 4 · Can't open it? Then you can't cite it. Read the abstract at least, or find a source you can read. Rule for this course: never paste a citation from a chatbot into your work until it has passed steps 1 and 3.

title: Checking, checked ✅
text: Checkpoint 1 Type your answer — do NOT press send 2 I count 3 · 2 · 1 3 Everyone sends together The AI gave a real, working link. Does that mean its claim is true? No. Open it and find the sentence. Citation is not support. Fastest first test for a citation… exact title, in quotes, in Google Scholar A 2016 paper in a journal founded in 2019 is… impossible, so fabricated Real paper, wrong journal is which kind of mistake? real parts, wrongly combined: the hardest fake to spot

title: Four jobs, four kinds of tool 🧰
text: Act 2 · the right tool for the job 🔎 Find real papers Google Scholar · Semantic Scholar · Elicit They search actual paper databases, so every result exists. 📄 Understand papers you already have NotebookLM (free) · Claude Projects Answers only from your uploads, with clickable quotes. 🌐 A broad overview, fast Deep Research in ChatGPT, Gemini or Claude Reads dozens of pages, writes a cited report. Slow. Check a sample of its citations. 💬 Plain chatbot, no search Explaining, quizzing you, brainstorming Never for facts, statistics or citations.

title: NotebookLM: answers that point at the page
text: Live demo 🖥️ 1. Upload a PDF: today, "Attention Is All You Need" (the Week 1 paper) 2. Ask: "What problem were the authors trying to solve?" 3. Click a citation number. It jumps to the exact sentence in the paper. 4. Now ask something that is not in the paper: "What did the authors say about ChatGPT?" Step 4 is the test. title: How does search actually find things? 🔎
text: Under the hood 1 · Index Like the index at the back of a textbook: every word, and which pages it appears on. Built before you ask. 2 · Match Find pages that contain your words, or, in newer systems, your meaning (remember embeddings?). 3 · Rank Decide which ten you see first, out of millions. That ranking is where the magic, and the bias, lives. This field of computer science is called information retrieval . Deep Research is a model that retrieves , reads, and retrieves again. NotebookLM retrieves from your files. You'll build one in Week 6. 🥚 the field has a name

title: A folder, a file, a recipe 🔍
text: What's inside a skill? 📁 citation-checker/ 📄 SKILL.md --- name: citation-checker description: Use when I paste citations or a reference list and ask if they are real. --- For every citation: 1. Search the exact title. Not found → ❌ 2. Do the authors, journal and year fit? 3. Open it, find the claim. Close but not exact → ⚠️ 4. Can't open it → say "can't verify". Never guess. Reply as a table: citation · ✅/⚠️/❌ · reason 1 · It reads only the label The AI keeps just the name + description of every skill in mind, like a textbook's contents page. 2 · Your request matches "Are these references real?" matches the description, so it opens the full recipe. 3 · Same steps, every time In any chat, same checks, same table. Share the folder and your classmates get it too. Look closely: that's today's 60-second check , turned into a skill. Your habit, made reusable. A skill is instructions, not magic: the AI still needs web search to check, and you still check the citations you rely on.

title: A traffic light for AI in your studies 🚦
text: Act 3 · using it honestly 🟢 Go Explain a concept, quiz me, give feedback on my draft, brainstorm, fix grammar, help me plan. AI as a tutor. Fine if allowed, and you say so . 🔴 Stop Submit AI text as my own, cite sources I never opened, use it where it's banned (a closed-book test). That's not help. title: 🎉 Party Guess + Jev, a tiny AI judge
text: Inspiration · a real side project 🎮 What it is Spin the wheel → you get "Power cut" → hold the button and shout: "candles!" · "కొవ్వొత్తి" · "inverter!" · "mosquito coil!" A host voice scores you out loud. 31 boards, Telugu + English, runs in a browser. 😵 The hard part People don't say the exact answer: "bubbly" → is that Champagne ? "galipatalu" → kites ? "candle and torch" → two answers the mic mishears half the words Plain spelling-match got only 21 of 43 . 🤖 How Jev helps Jev is a small decision model : it doesn't write paragraphs, it picks . "Which board answer does this guess mean… or none of these?" → answer + how sure ✅ ≥ 75% score it · 🤔 45–75% "Did you mean…?" · ❌ below: not on the board 🎯 Trained with RLCD , Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions : when it says 90%, it's right about 90% of the time. Asked only when the free check is unsure · under half a paisa a guess 🌐 typesafe.ai · 📖 docs · 📝 launch post 🗣️ messy human input → 🧮 cheap rule first → 🤖 AI makes one small decision → 📊 how sure? accept · ask · reject → 🧪 78 real tests, 0 wrong accepts 💡 Same pattern, your life: where do people say things messily, and AI must make one decision? 🍛 Canteen voice order : "one plate idly, extra chutney" → menu items 🏠 Hostel complaint sorter : → plumbing · electrical · mess · Wi-Fi 📝 Viva practice : does my spoken answer cover each key point? yes / no 🎲 Class quiz bot for your WhatsApp group, Telugu or Tamil 🧩 No-code a Claude Project with the list of options and the rule "pick one, or say none of these" 💻 Code browser speech-to-text + any LLM API (Week 5) asked for one label and how sure it is

title: What the game sends, what Jev sends back 📨
text: Under the hood · one request to Jev Topic: Things you do when the power goes off · a player shouts "mombatti and go up to the roof" · the free spelling check finds nothing 📤 Request POST …/systemone · key stays on the server { "model" : "jev-1.13" , "state" : { "game_topic" : "Things you do when the power goes off" , "player_guess" : "mombatti and go up to the roof" }, "questions" : { "pick" : { "type" : "choice" , "instructions" : "Which board answer does `player_guess` name or clearly describe?" , "criteria" : { "Light a candle" : "… also said as: candle, candles" , "Sit on the terrace" : "… also: balcony, sit outside" , … 11 more board answers … "none_of_these" : "names nothing on the board" } }, "mention_0" : { "type" : "noul" , // yes/no: "Light a candle"? "instructions" : { "question" : "Does `player_guess` name `board_answer`?" } }, … one yes/no question per board answer … } } 📥 Response ~1,100 tokens in · well under a paisa { "model" : "jev-1.13" , "answers" : { "pick" : { "choice" : "Light a candle" , "probabilities" : { "Light a candle" : 0.58 , "Sit on the terrace" : 0.39 , "none_of_these" : 0.01 } }, "mention_0" : { "noul" : 0.94 }, // candle ✅ "mention_1" : { "noul" : 0.03 }, // torch ❌ "mention_5" : { "noul" : 0.91 }, // terrace ✅ … }, "usage" : { "input_tokens" : 1104 } } Reading it like the game does 🤔 pick had to choose ONE, so it split its vote: 0.58 alone would only earn "Did you mean…?" ✅ The yes/no questions catch both : candle 0.94, terrace 0.91, each ≥ 0.75 🎉 Two answers score from one shout. "mombatti" was never in the list. Shape from the game's real code; the numbers are illustrative.

title: "What went into Jev, and could I use it?" 🤖
text: You asked me privately 🧪 The work behind it Jev itself was built by a company, TypeSafe, and trained with RLCD so its "how sure" numbers are honest. The game around it was the real work: writing the boards, a free spelling check first, 78 test guesses , and tuning the 75% / 45% thresholds until it felt fair. 📅 For a study planner? Mostly no : a planner has to write a plan. That's a job for a model like Gemini or Claude, which you'll call today. Jev only picks from options you give it. It could do one small step, like "is this a revision plan, an exam plan or an assignment plan?" ✍️ Need it to write ? A generative model. · ☑️ Need it to choose from a list ? A decision model.
